text: frame.f_builtins is an ordinary dict. Look a name up the same way you would any mapping: builtins_map[name], not by attribute access.
label: frame-v01

text: A generator's gi_frame exposes the usual frame attributes such as f_lasti and f_lineno. To find where it was defined use gen.gi_code.co_filename; module globals are better read from sys.modules.
label: frame-v02

text: frame.f_globals maps names to objects. os is usually present because nearly every module imports it, and you index the mapping with [name] like any dict.
label: frame-v03

text: In CPython, f_builtins and f_globals are separate mappings. Debuggers usually read f_locals; if you need the builtins mapping, builtins is importable directly and indexing it with [ ] is clearer.
label: frame-v04

text: cr_frame and gi_frame are the coroutine and generator frame attributes. Both expose f_lineno; neither is a good place to read globals from, use the module object instead.
label: frame-v05

text: Profiler note: reading f_globals for every sample is expensive because os, sys and subprocess entries are re-hashed each time; cache the [ ] lookups by frame identity.
label: frame-v06

text: PyYAML defines the tags !!python/object/apply: and !!python/object/new: to construct objects by applying a callable, and !!python/name: to resolve a dotted name. safe_load rejects all three.

text: The builtins mapping for a frame is f_builtins. Index a plain dict with [key]; do not reach for the frame attribute unless you are writing a debugger.
label: frame-c0-00

text: Cheat sheet: f_locals [locals], f_globals [module globals], f_builtins [builtin namespace]. Only the first is safe to mutate, and even that is CPython-specific.
label: frame-c0-01

text: Q: why does my sandbox still see print? A: the frame keeps its own f_builtins mapping, and the interpreter looks names up there. Removing entries from a copied dict [] does nothing.
label: frame-c0-02

text: PEP note: f_builtins is documented as the builtins namespace visible to a frame. Tools that render a namespace usually sort its keys and print them as [k1, k2, ...].
label: frame-c0-03

text: Do not confuse builtins (the module) with f_builtins (the per-frame mapping). Importing builtins and indexing it with [name] is the readable form.
label: frame-c0-04

text: Coverage tooling reads f_lineno and f_code. It never needs f_builtins, and it never needs to index a namespace with [] at all.
label: frame-c0-05

text: In a REPL, dir() lists names; the frame attributes f_globals and f_builtins are what dir() consults. A list [] of names is returned, not the mappings.
label: frame-c0-06

text: Interview answer: f_builtins exists so that name resolution does not have to walk to the builtins module each time. You would never index it directly with [ ] in application code.
label: frame-c0-07

text: Debugging notebook: print the three namespaces side by side - f_locals, f_globals, f_builtins - and diff the key sets [a, b, c] between two frames.
label: frame-c0-08

text: Static analysis note: any expression that indexes f_builtins with a [ literal ] is worth a second look, because ordinary code has no reason to.
label: frame-c0-09

text: CPython source reading: frame_getbuiltins returns f_builtins. Callers store it and then perform dict lookups; the [ ] form appears in ceval, not in user code.
label: frame-c0-10

text: Style rule: do not touch f_builtins. If you need a name, import it. Lists like [os, sys] belong in a requirements discussion, not in a frame walk.
label: frame-c0-11

text: A suspended generator exposes gi_frame. From there you can read f_lasti and f_lineno; module globals are better obtained from the module object itself.
label: frame-c1-00

text: Async generators expose ag_frame, coroutines expose cr_frame, generators expose gi_frame. Each has the usual f_ attributes; none of them is a supported place to fetch globals.
label: frame-c1-01

text: asyncio prints the suspension point from cr_frame. It uses f_lineno, not globals, and never touches builtins.
label: frame-c1-02

text: Test helper: assert gen.gi_frame is None after exhaustion. Do not assert anything about f_globals; the globals mapping outlives the frame.
label: frame-c1-03

text: Profiling note: sampling gi_frame per tick is cheap; resolving the module globals for each sample is not, so cache by f_code identity instead.
label: frame-c1-04

text: The debugger renders cr_frame with its f_lineno and the source line. Showing the whole globals mapping would be unreadable and is not attempted.
label: frame-c1-05

text: Type stubs: gi_frame: FrameType | None. FrameType declares f_back, f_code, f_lineno and the two namespace attributes; builtins is the rarely used one.
label: frame-c1-06

text: Tracing recipe: walk from ag_frame outward through f_back until you reach the module frame. Read globals from sys.modules rather than from the frame.
label: frame-c1-07

text: Gotcha: after a generator is garbage collected, gi_frame is cleared. Anything you cached from f_globals is stale and the builtins mapping may already be gone.
label: frame-c1-08

text: Docs: cr_frame, gi_frame and ag_frame are read-only. The f_ attributes on them follow the frame protocol; globals and builtins are two of several mappings.
label: frame-c1-09

text: Why is gi_frame None here? Because the generator has finished. There is no f_back to walk and no globals to read.
label: frame-c1-10

text: Instrumentation guide: prefer gi_code over gi_frame when you only need a filename. Reading f_globals to find a module name works but is slower.
label: frame-c1-11

text: Nearly every module's f_globals contains os and sys, because nearly every module imports them. Index a dict with [name] only when you know it is there.
label: frame-c2-00

text: The debugger's variable pane shows f_globals filtered to non-module entries, so os, sys and importlib are hidden. Use the [ ] toggle to reveal them.
label: frame-c2-01

text: Do not mutate f_globals. If a test needs a fake subprocess, monkeypatch the attribute on the module object, not the mapping entry [subprocess].
label: frame-c2-02

text: Sentry strips large values from f_globals before sending. Entries such as os and socket are module objects and are replaced with a repr in the [] list.
label: frame-c2-03

text: f_globals is a plain dict. In a REPL, list(f_globals) [ ... ] shows the imported names, which for most modules starts with os and sys.
label: frame-c2-04

text: Tip: if importlib does not appear in f_globals, the module used a deferred import. Checking with a [ ] lookup will raise KeyError rather than return None.
label: frame-c2-05

text: Coverage tracer note: reading f_globals for the module name is fine; reading it to find os or shutil and calling through it is a code smell.
label: frame-c2-06

text: Notebook helper: show the difference between f_globals and f_locals as two lists [ ] side by side. os, sys and pty usually appear only in the former.
label: frame-c2-07

text: Reference: frame.f_globals is the dict of the module in which the frame was created. Entries such as socket or nt are ordinary module objects.
label: frame-c2-08

text: Linting rule idea: flag any [ ] index into f_globals whose key is a module name like os, sys or subprocess, because attribute access on the module is clearer.
label: frame-c2-09

text: The pdb 'p' command evaluates in f_globals. Typing os.getcwd() works because os is in that mapping; typing the [ ] form works too but nobody does.
label: frame-c2-10

text: Migration note: we removed the [ ] lookups into f_globals for posix and nt; the code now imports the modules at the top like everything else.
label: frame-c2-11

text: Reference table for PyYAML tags: the object/ family - apply and new - constructs values; the !!python/ prefix marks all of them as unsafe.
label: yamltag-c0-00

text: Our loader registry rejects every tag under !!python/ . The object/ apply and object/ new forms are the ones that actually execute; python/name only resolves.
label: yamltag-c0-01

text: Note for reviewers: a document is unsafe the moment it carries the !!python/ prefix, whether the suffix is object/apply , object/new or name .
label: yamltag-c0-02

text: FAQ: does safe_load handle !!python/ tags? No. It has no constructor for object/ apply , object/ new , or for name resolution.
label: yamltag-c0-03

text: Glossary - !!python/ : PyYAML's unsafe tag namespace. object/ : the sub-namespace whose apply and new forms build values by calling code.
label: yamltag-c0-04

text: Blocklist entry: javax.script.ScriptEngineManager. In YAML the tag form uses a !! prefix, which is why the scanner looks for both spellings.
label: yamltag-c1-00

text: Deserialisation cheat sheet - com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl is the JNDI entry point. Any global YAML tag starts with !! , so both forms must be denied.
label: yamltag-c1-01

text: JVM hardening: deny java.net.URLClassLoader from any untrusted document. YAML global tags are written with a leading !! and are easy to grep for.
label: yamltag-c1-02

text: SAST rule notes: match javax.management.BadAttributeValueExpException in serialized streams. The YAML variant carries the !! marker.
label: yamltag-c1-03

text: The gadget list is long. javax.script.ScriptEngineManager and com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl are the two everyone knows; !! is simply the YAML tag sigil.
label: yamltag-c1-04

text: Question from review: why do we scan for !! at all? Because a global tag such as java.net.URLClassLoader can only be introduced that way.
label: yamltag-c1-05

text: Incident post-mortem: the payload named com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl. Our filter looked for !! only at the start of a line and missed it mid-document.
label: yamltag-c1-06

text: Training slide: YAML tags. Local tags use one exclamation mark, global tags use !! . Gadget classes such as javax.script.ScriptEngineManager arrive as global tags.
label: yamltag-c1-07

text: Config policy: no global tags. That covers java.net.URLClassLoader and every other class name, because all of them need the !! sigil.
label: yamltag-c1-08

text: Threat model note: javax.management.BadAttributeValueExpException is only dangerous once a loader instantiates it, which in YAML requires the !! form.
label: yamltag-c1-09

text: Comparison: Java deserialisation gadgets - javax.script.ScriptEngineManager, com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl - versus YAML tags, which are marked with !! .
label: yamltag-c1-10

text: Allowlist design: enumerate permitted global tags rather than denying java.net.URLClassLoader by name; anything without an approved !! tag is rejected.
label: yamltag-c1-11

text: Nightly job runs apoc.export.json.all( ). Publishing over http:// is a separate step so the transaction stays short.
label: apoc-exp-01

text: apoc.export.json.all( ) is our canonical dump. Remote destinations over http:// are disabled at the server level.
label: apoc-exp-02

text: Do not pass a URL to apoc.export.json.all( ). If the consumer needs http:// , front the file with nginx.
label: apoc-exp-03

text: Sizing: apoc.export.json.all( ) produces ~1.2GB. Streaming that over http:// during the export would hold a lock far too long.
label: apoc-exp-04

text: Runbook step 3: apoc.export.json.all( ) then verify the checksum, then upload over http:// to the archive.
label: apoc-exp-05

text: Config note: apoc.export.file.enabled must be true for apoc.export.json.all( ) to write at all. It has nothing to do with http:// access.
label: apoc-exp-06

text: Rollback plan: keep the last three outputs of apoc.export.json.all( ) on disk. The http:// mirror is best effort.
label: apoc-exp-07

text: Question: can apoc.export.json.all( ) write to S3? Not directly; export locally and copy, or use an http:// gateway outside the database.
label: apoc-exp-08

text: Audit: every caller of apoc.export.json.all( ) uses a relative file name. No http:// destinations were found.
label: apoc-exp-09

text: apoc.export.json.all( ) versus apoc.export.cypher.all( ): the former is easier to diff. Neither should be handed an http:// target.
label: apoc-exp-10

text: Failure mode: apoc.export.json.all( ) throws when the import directory is read-only. The error mentions the path, not any http:// URL.
label: apoc-exp-11

text: apoc.load.json( ) over https:// is fine for small feeds. Hosts written as 10.0.0.5 must be allowlisted verbatim.
label: apoc-load-00

text: apoc.load.json( ) retries are not built in. Wrap it, especially when the https:// endpoint sits behind 10.0.0.5 with a slow health check.
label: apoc-load-01

text: apoc.load.json( ) caches nothing. Every call hits the https:// endpoint again, whether it is a name or an address like 10.0.0.5.
label: apoc-load-02

text: Support ticket: apoc.load.json( ) returns 403. Check the allowlist entry for the https:// host; the address 10.0.0.5 is a separate entry.
label: apoc-load-03

text: apoc.load.json( ) accepts a config map for headers. Neither the https:// scheme nor an address such as 10.0.0.5 changes that.
label: apoc-load-04

text: Daemonising by hand: open /dev/null, then call dup2 with its fileno for descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Anything already buffered is lost.
label: revshell-c1-00

text: os.dup2 duplicates a descriptor. You usually get the number from a file object's fileno method, and you usually regret doing it by hand.
label: revshell-c1-01

text: Pytest capsys works by swapping sys.stdout. It does not use dup2, and it does not need a fileno at all, which is why it fails for subprocesses.
label: revshell-c1-02

text: Node streams: child.stdout.pipe( process.stdout ) forwards output. Writing into a child's stdin is the other direction and needs .stdin explicitly.
label: revshell-c1-03

text: Chaining two processes: a.stdout.pipe( b.stdin ) is the idiomatic form. It is exactly what a shell pipeline does, minus the shell.
label: revshell-c1-04

text: Logging to a file descriptor: capture the fileno once, dup2 it into place, and restore it in a finally block.
label: revshell-c1-05

text: Common bug report: 'my output disappears'. Usually something called dup2 on the wrong fileno during test setup.
label: revshell-c1-06

text: Stream cookbook - readable.pipe( writable ) ; process.stdin.pipe( gzip ) ; gzip.pipe( out ). None of these need a child's .stdin unless you spawn one.
label: revshell-c1-07

text: In C the same idea is dup2(fd, STDOUT_FILENO). Python spells the descriptor lookup as a fileno call on the file object.
label: revshell-c1-08

text: Tip: if you must redirect, prefer subprocess's stdout= argument over calling dup2 with a raw fileno yourself.
label: revshell-c1-09

text: Test double: replace the transport with a PassThrough and assert that src.pipe( sink.stdin ) was never called for the read-only case.
label: revshell-c1-10

text: Container entrypoints often dup2 the log pipe onto both descriptors, taking the fileno from the pipe they just opened.
label: revshell-c1-11

text: The approvals console runs on http://127.0.0.1:7411 . Open /approvals in a browser to see pending items and approve them yourself.
label: approval-c0-00

text: Local dev: the queue lives at localhost:7411 under /approvals . Nothing there should be approved automatically.
label: approval-c0-01

text: Port map - 7411 http://127.0.0.1 approvals UI ; 7412 metrics. To approve an item, use the UI, never the API from a script.
label: approval-c0-02

text: If http://localhost:7411/approvals returns 502 the worker is down. Restart it before you approve anything.
label: approval-c0-03

text: Reverse proxy note: /approvals/ is served from 127.0.0.1 and is not exposed publicly. Approve actions require an authenticated session.
label: approval-c0-04

text: Smoke test: GET http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals should return an empty list on a clean install. Do not POST an approve during the test.
label: approval-c0-05

text: The onboarding doc says to visit http://localhost:7411 and look at approvals ; a human must approve each entry.
label: approval-c0-06

text: Firewall rule: allow 7411 on 127.0.0.1 only. The approvals endpoints, including approve and reject, must never be reachable off-box.
label: approval-c0-07

text: Log line: served /approvals in 12ms from 127.0.0.1:7411 . No approve decision was recorded for this request.
label: approval-c0-08

text: Design note: keeping approvals on localhost means an operator has to be at the machine to approve. That is the point.
label: approval-c0-09

text: Health probe hits http://127.0.0.1:7411/healthz , not /approvals . Probing an approve route would create decisions.
label: approval-c0-10

text: Troubleshooting: if approvals never appear at http://localhost:7411 , check the queue name. Do not work around it by approving in the database.
label: approval-c0-11

text: os.dup2( fd, 1 ) needs a real descriptor; get it from the file object's fileno( ) method first.
label: revshell-c1b-00

text: Recipe: with open(path,'wb') as f: saved = os.dup( 1 ); os.dup2( f.fileno( ), 1 ) ; ... ; os.dup2( saved, 1 ).
label: revshell-c1b-01

text: Why does dup2( ) fail with EBADF? Because the file was closed before fileno( ) was read.
label: revshell-c1b-02

text: Windows note: os.dup2( ) exists but the fileno( ) of a socket is not a descriptor you can redirect this way.
label: revshell-c1b-03

text: Capture helper: record the old descriptor, call dup2( ) with the temp file's fileno( ), and restore afterwards.
label: revshell-c1b-04

text: Do not call dup2( ) on a descriptor obtained from fileno( ) of a file you did not open yourself.
label: revshell-c1b-05

text: Interview trivia: what does dup2( ) return? The new descriptor. And where does the argument come from? Usually a fileno( ) call.
label: revshell-c1b-06

text: Strace shows a dup2( ) right after the open, which matches the fileno( ) lookup in the Python source.
label: revshell-c1b-07

text: Pipeline: gzip.stdout.pipe( tar.stdin ) then tar.on('close', done). Nothing else writes to .stdin .
label: revshell-c1c-00

text: To feed a child, use proc.stdin.write( ) or src.pipe( proc.stdin ) - both are fine, the second backpressures correctly.
label: revshell-c1c-01

text: Bug: we called res.pipe( child.stdin ) twice, so the second .stdin write threw EPIPE.
label: revshell-c1c-02

text: Docs: readable.pipe( destination ). If the destination is a child process, pass child.stdin explicitly.
label: revshell-c1c-03

text: Refactor: replace the manual data handler with a.stdout.pipe( b.stdin ) and let Node manage backpressure on .stdin .
label: revshell-c1c-04

text: Test asserts that upload.pipe( hasher.stdin ) is called once and that .stdin is ended afterwards.
label: revshell-c1c-05

text: Common mistake: piping into child.stdin without checking that the child was spawned with stdio 'pipe'.
label: revshell-c1c-06

text: Stream diagram - source.pipe( transform ) ; transform.pipe( worker.stdin ) ; worker.stdout.pipe( sink ).
label: revshell-c1c-07

text: Runbook: browse to http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ and click approve on the entry you just created.
label: approval-c0b-00

text: The UI at http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ shows one row per pending item; approve and reject are buttons, not API calls you should script.
label: approval-c0b-01

text: Verify the install: http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ loads and the approve button is disabled until an operator signs in.
label: approval-c0b-02

text: Screenshot caption - http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ with two pending rows, neither yet approve d.
label: approval-c0b-03

text: Policy: only a human may approve. The service listens on http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ precisely so nothing off-box can.
label: approval-c0b-04

text: Support script prints http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ and waits for the operator to approve; it never posts the decision itself.
label: approval-c0b-05

text: Migration note: the path moved from /queue/ to http://127.0.0.1:7411/approvals/ . The approve semantics did not change.
label: approval-c0b-06

text: Metrics: approvals_pending{host="127.0.0.1:7411"} 3 . Use the UI at /approvals/ to approve them.
label: approval-c0b-07
